title: Plan 9 from Outer Space

evidence.note: The Public Domain Review page, titled 'Plan 9 From Outer Space (1959)', shows two rights labels: 'PD U.S.' for the underlying work and 'Unclear' for the digital copy. Under 'Unclear' it says the Internet Archive has a CC BY-NC-SA default 'which this might fall under'. The page mentions no copyright registration or renewal. Term rule: a US work first published in 1957 through 1963 keeps protection for 95 years only if a renewal was filed in the 28th year. The year of first publication is unresolved: it may be 1957 (preview), 1958 (release) or 1959 (other labels). For a first publication in 1957, 1958 or 1959, renewal would fall in the 28th year, which is 1985-87. Without a renewal it fell into the public domain. We did not find a renewal record, so no primary record settles the question.

Catalog of Copyright Entries, Third Series, Parts 12-13: Motion Pictures and Filmstrips, Jan-Dec 1958 (archive.org identifier catalogofcopyrig3121213li). Only the first 100,000 characters of a text of roughly 913,000 characters were read, and nothing for this film turned up in that part. The 1957, 1958 (remainder) and 1959 registration volumes and the 1985-87 renewal volumes all remain unsearched. This is not a complete search, and it does not show that a registration or renewal exists or does not exist.
evidence.source: Internet Archive / Library of Congress Copyright Office

evidence.note: A real, confirmed post-1978 record exists: PA0000102338, filed 1981-04-23, 'Plan 9 from outer space / written, produced, directed by Edward D. Wood, Jr.', claimant Reynolds Pictures, Inc. (distributor Wade Williams's company), registered as a work made for hire. Secondary discussion (an archive.org forum thread examining this same registration) argues the claim is legally shaky: the project originated with Ed Wood independently, with Reynolds coming in later as a backer rather than an employer, which is at odds with a work-for-hire basis. Separately, a later renewal of the film has been pursued through Kathy Wood (Ed Wood's widow), whose standing to transfer his rights is itself disputed in that same secondary discussion. No renewal registration number for either claim could be independently verified in this pass, and none is asserted here. This dispute is why the print stays undetermined rather than being called free or protected.
evidence.source: U.S. Copyright Office Public Records System (PA0000102338); archive.org forum discussion of the registration

evidence.note: Further secondary discussion of this same dispute.
evidence.source: archive.org forum — "more to come: plan 9 from outer space copyright"

evidence.note: The soundtrack follows the film's own status, which is undetermined (see the print layer). Wikipedia's article on the film says: 'The music for Plan 9 from Outer Space was compiled by Gordon Zahler. Zahler had taken over the stock-music library of his late father Lee Zahler.' Those compositions and recordings may have their own copyright histories. Check them before licensing the music for new synchronization or commercial release.
We found nothing showing the film was adapted from an earlier published work, but we did not run a search for one. The story takes the film's own status, which is undetermined (see the print layer).
USPTO trademark databases could not be searched in this session. We know of no active mark for 'Plan 9 from Outer Space', but trademark status stays undetermined until a USPTO search is done.

A faithful restoration of a public-domain film adds no new US copyright. Slavish reproduction of public-domain images without original creative additions is not protected (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., S.D.N.Y. 1999, following Feist v. Rural, 1991). Original additions can be protected. The Internet Archive item includes a colourised version, and colorization can carry its own protection. Wikipedia reports that Turner Classic Movies released a high-definition transfer in 1.85:1 widescreen, with stock footage shots adjusted for framing, so such releases may add protectable material. Use archival prints rather than ripping a commercial disc, because ripping a copy-protected disc can implicate 17 U.S.C. § 1201.
evidence.source: Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp.

evidence.note: 17 U.S.C. § 1201 — DMCA anti-circumvention prohibition on defeating technological protection measures.

editorial:
Plan 9 from Outer Space is a science-fiction horror film made by Ed Wood. Wikipedia reports that it was shot in black and white in November 1956 and had a preview screening at the Carlton Theatre in Los Angeles on March 15, 1957, under the title Grave Robbers from Outer Space. It also says the film went into general release in July 1958 in Virginia, Texas and several other Southern states. Other sources, including the Public Domain Review and Internet Archive titles, label it 1959, so the dates differ by source. The Public Domain Review lists the film as 'PD U.S.' but mentions no registration or renewal, and it marks the digital copy's rights as 'Unclear'.

The rights trap is that nobody has shown the status with a primary record, and there is a live dispute rather than a settled gap. A work first published in 1957 to 1963 stays protected for 95 years only if it was renewed in the 28th year. Because first publication may be 1957, 1958 or 1959, renewal for any of these would fall in 1985-87. We read only part of the 1958 motion-picture volume of the Catalog of Copyright Entries and found nothing there. The 1957, 1958 (remainder) and 1959 registration volumes and the 1985-87 renewal volumes all remain unsearched. What we did confirm is a 1981 work-for-hire registration (PA0000102338) filed by Reynolds Pictures, Inc. (distributor Wade Williams's company) and secondary discussion arguing that claim, and a separate later renewal pursued through Kathy Wood, are both contested rather than confirmed. That contested ownership, not just an unsearched volume, is why the print stays undetermined. The soundtrack is also a compilation. Per Wikipedia, Gordon Zahler compiled it, and he had taken over his late father Lee Zahler's stock-music library, so those tracks may have their own histories. The Internet Archive upload's title mentions a colourised version, but we could not verify who made it or when, so the restoration layer stays undetermined. Treat the film as unverified until a full registration and renewal search is done, and get advice before reusing footage commercially.
faq: Can I use Plan 9 from Outer Space footage in my own film or video?

Not safely, as far as we can verify. The Public Domain Review lists the film as 'PD U.S.', but its page mentions no registration or renewal search. We searched only part of one catalog volume and found no primary record either way. The status is undetermined until a full Copyright Office registration and renewal search is done. Get advice before reusing footage commercially.
Does an Internet Archive copy or a Creative Commons label mean I can reuse it?

No. A hosting label on an uploaded copy does not decide the film's copyright status. The Public Domain Review marks the digital copy's rights as 'Unclear' and notes the Internet Archive's CC BY-NC-SA default. Added material such as a colourised version or a new score can also be protected on its own, and we could not verify the provenance of the colourised upload.
